myth: Paying cash is the safe way to invest.
reality: We’d usually borrow for the asset and keep the cash working.
because: The property grows the same whether or not it carries a loan. Borrowed money isn’t income, and your cash stays where you can reach it. Run it with your accountant.

myth: It’s interest-free, so it doesn’t count.
reality: The bank counts the repayment, not the interest.
because: Every monthly commitment comes off what you can borrow, interest or not. Small buy-now-pay-later and store facilities quietly cap a refinance or a second purchase.

myth: You need ten percent on the contract.
reality: The contract deposit is a negotiation, not a rule.
because: With solid pre-approval, a smaller deposit, a staged deposit or a deposit bond can all work. We’d rather that than drain a parent’s savings to look strong.

myth: The tax return will soften the holding cost.
reality: On an older property, there’s little depreciation to claim.
because: Established homes bring very little depreciation, so the after-tax cost sits close to the pre-tax number. We model it that way. Check what’s realistic with your accountant.

myth: Buy an investment first and you lose your first home benefits.
reality: Sometimes. It depends on your state and whether you live there.
because: In some states an investment you never live in doesn’t burn every first home concession. The rules differ and change, so we check before you sign.

myth: A bigger deposit means less stamp duty.
reality: Duty is set by the property, not the loan.
because: Transfer duty depends on the type and price of the property and your eligibility as a buyer. Borrowing less or putting in more changes nothing on that bill.

myth: Sell the home and the bank will lend me more.
reality: Selling gives you cash, not borrowing power.
because: The rent you pay afterwards goes straight back into the servicing calculation. Capacity comes from income and lower commitments, not from turning an asset into a bank balance.

myth: Refinancing means moving everything to one bank.
reality: Different banks win at different things. We often use two.
because: One lender might be sharpest on rate for the refinance. Another lends more when capacity matters for the next purchase. Pick the lender for the job in front of you.

myth: The bank’s valuation is what the house is worth.
reality: It’s a lending number. The sale price is a different number.
because: We’ll push a valuation as hard as we can to get a refinance through, and still tell you plainly what the market would pay if you sold.

myth: My repayment didn’t drop, so the offset isn’t working.
reality: The offset cuts your interest, not your repayment. That’s the point.
because: The same repayment now clears more principal, so you finish years earlier. Look at the interest line on your statement, not the repayment, and check the offset is linked.

myth: One bank said no, so that’s the answer.
reality: Borrowing power isn’t one number. It depends who you ask.
because: The same payslips through different lenders’ calculators give different answers. We run several before we tell anyone a number, usually within a day of getting documents.

myth: Interest-only is the cheaper way to hold a property.
reality: It usually carries a higher rate. It’s a tool, not a default.
because: Interest-only buys cash-flow room when you need it. If the rent covers principal and interest comfortably, paying it down is cheaper and faster. Ask for both figures.

myth: I’m pre-approved, so the loan is approved.
reality: Only if a human actually read your file.
because: Some pre-approvals are system-generated with conditions buried in the fine print, and fall over when you buy. We insist on one a credit assessor has looked at.

myth: The grant is part of my deposit.
reality: We plan settlement as if the grant won’t arrive.
because: Grants can be reassessed or declined at the last minute. If the settlement figures relied on that money, the shortfall comes from your pocket on the day.

myth: Going guarantor is just a signature from Mum and Dad.
reality: Their house is committed for years, not just your deposit.
because: If the guarantors sell before their home is released as security, a cash contribution is usually required. The whole family needs to agree on the timeline before anyone signs.
